Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)IPTC photo metadata

IPTC photo metadata tests are the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's tests of what sharing sites and systems do to the metadata embedded in a photograph: upload, view, save, download, then check whether its Exif and IPTC fields survive (2013, 2016, 2019). The IPTC Photo Metadata Standard they test is a distinct object (2019 page; census record).

🧪 The tests

  • What they check: the IPTC's claim that "embedded metadata should not be removed"; the 4Cs (caption, creator, copyright notice, credit line) shown and kept (2019 page; census record).3↘
    The IPTC photo metadata tests are the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's checks of what image-sharing sites and systems for sharing files and messages do to the metadata embedded in an uploaded photograph: the IPTC "checks about a dozen sites regularly: in 2013, in 2016 and now again in Spring 2019," each time against its own claim that "embedded metadata should not be removed" from shared images (IPTC, Social Media Sites Photo Metadata Test Results 2019), and the provenance census record names the series, gives its operator as the IPTC's Photo Metadata Working Group, and records that it both expresses and tests provenance (provenance census record).§1 Each test uploads an image whose embedded values are all known, "e.g. the latest Reference Image File," checks what the site displays, saves the image with the browser's Save As and downloads it through the system, and asks of each file whether "the embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (in the formats IIM and XMP) of the uploaded image" are "still embedded" (2019 page); the census record keeps the same operations as the transformations tested, embedded metadata inside the file as the carrier, and the site or system as the unit (provenance census record).§2 Four fields are checked on display, "Caption/description, Creator, Copyright Notice, Credit Line (= the 4Cs )" (2019 page), which the census record carries as the relations tested: creation, credit, rights and description (provenance census record).§3
  • Origin: users' embedded metadata "disappeared" when shared; 15 sites tested in 2013 and 2016, about a dozen in 2019 (Research page; census record).2↘
    The IPTC gives the series its origin: users "discovered that when they shared photos via social media sites or systems, their embedded metadata disappeared," and the Working Group "tested 15 social media sites in 2016 and 2013 to understand how image sharing, through upload and download, affects the integrity of embedded metadata" (IPTC, Photo Metadata Research).§4 The census record dates the series to 2013, 2016 and Spring 2019, with a software test published in August 2014, counts 15 sites in 2016 and 2013 and about a dozen in 2019, and was read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).§6

📉 What they found

  • 2019: Pexels, pixabay, Unsplash strip saved and downloaded files; Flickr swaps in the account owner as creator; Twitter strips; Facebook keeps a few rights fields; Behance keeps them (2019 page; census record).3↘
    In the Spring 2019 tables Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash strip the metadata from saved and downloaded files, and on Flickr the "Embedded Creator" is "replaced by account owner" while saved files lose their XMP (2019 page).§7 Among the systems for sharing files and messages, Facebook keeps "A few rights related fields" in IIM and Exif and writes two IIM fields of its own, Twitter strips saved files, and Dropbox and OneDrive pass the original through while their previews save "with stripped off metadata"; Behance's saved files "keep the embedded metadata" (2019 page).§8 The census record keeps the same year and the same losses as its retention results: of eleven image-sharing sites, Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripping, Flickr replacing the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripping on Save As, Facebook keeping a few rights fields (provenance census record).§9
  • Reading: "not impossible to preserve metadata in a workflow"; a 2014 study found rights fields in half the programs (Research page).1↘
    The research page reads the series as showing that some sites "remove embedded information like copyright notes, the name of the creator, the description and more, while others protect photographers’ data better," and that "it is not impossible to preserve metadata in a workflow"; its software study of August 2014 found rights fields in half of the programs tested, retrieval of embedded rights data in two out of three, and two programs that "didn’t support rights metadata at all" (Research page).§10
  • Beyond platforms: DAMs, CMSs and CDNs strip too, against the IPTC's rule that rights metadata "must never be removed" (User Guide; FAQ; NeededApps).2↘
    The norm the tests measure is the IPTC's own: its User Guide endorses the Embedded Metadata Manifesto, under which "Copyright management information metadata must never be removed from the files," removal being "forbidden by law in many countries," and its minimum set of fields "is not a permission to strip off metadata" (IPTC Photo Metadata User Guide, November 2025).§11 The same guide and the IPTC's Google Images FAQ place the loss also in the sites that host images: a site's "digital asset management system, content management system, image management system or content delivery network may be stripping out embedded metadata fields" (User Guide), the metadata "might be stripped from your images by some software on your site," a DAM, a CMS such as WordPress or Drupal, or a CDN such as Cloudflare (FAQ), and NeededApps' explainer holds that metadata is no "infallible form of copyright protection because it can be removed or modified" (NeededApps).§12
  • The archive: in-pixel metadata survives the stripping embedded metadata does not; publication-layer signals are stripped before training: "The body text is what survives" (#1409; #127).1↘
    The archive reads the same loss at other carriers and stages: in-pixel metadata "survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss," so the archive's handwritten artifacts carry their metadata three times, "in the pixels + embedded (IPTC/XMP/C2PA) + external" (#1409), and the publication layer's provenance signals, C2PA manifests and structured metadata among them, "are stripped or rendered invisible long before they reach the training corpus. The body text is what survives" (#127).§13

📐 The standard they test

  • What it is: Core and Extension properties (administrative, descriptive, rights), from the 1990s IIM, embedded as IIM and XMP; 2025.1: Core 1.5, Extension 1.9 (IPTC; Wikipedia).3↘
    The object the tests test is a distinct entity, the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard, which "sets the industry standard for administrative, descriptive, and copyright information about images" (IPTC, Photo Metadata): its properties are grouped "into Administrative, Descriptive and Rights-related properties" (Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1) in two schemas, IPTC Core and IPTC Extension, "built on the legacy of the original IPTC-IIM" (IPTC Photo Metadata Standard page), and the census record gives the object they bear on as "the photograph as a file: embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (IIM and XMP)" (provenance census record).§14 Its current release is 2025.1, "including … IPTC Core Metadata Schema 1.5 … IPTC Extension Metadata Schema 1.9" (specification, About the Standard), while the same specification heads its Extension section "IPTC Extension schema 1.8 specifications" (specification, contents and body).§15 Its genealogy runs from the IIM, "developed in the early 1990s by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) to expedite the international exchange of news" (Wikipedia, IPTC Information Interchange Model), whose image properties were embedded as the "IPTC header" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council; Wikipedia, IIM), to XMP, which "has largely superseded IIM's file structure" (Wikipedia, IIM), the IPTC having worked "alongside Adobe" on an implementation that "employs Adobe’s XMP technology" (Standard page); Core fields embedded in both formats must have their values synchronised by the image software (User Guide).§16
  • AI fields: four 2025.1 properties for AI-generated content; writing them invalidated an image's C2PA metadata (IPTC news).2↘
    The 2025.1 release, announced by the Working Group on 27 November 2025, adds four properties "for AI-generated content", AI Prompt Information, AI Prompt Writer Name, AI System Used and AI System Version Used, the third defined as "The AI engine and/or the model name used to generate this image" (IPTC news; Standard page), beside the Data Mining property, a "Data mining prohibition or permission, optionally with constraints" (specification).§20 The User Guide gives their purpose, to tell AI-generated images from "regular" ones "to avoid re-training AI models on content that was already generated by a model," and recommends leaving Image Creator empty and setting Digital Source Type to trainedAlgorithmicMedia or compositeSynthetic (User Guide); the announcement records that writing the new properties into its example image "has rendered the C2PA metadata invalid" (IPTC news), and the census record marks the tests "NOT a test of C2PA credentials" (provenance census record).§21
  • The archive: IPTC AI metadata is "Layer 1 metadata", "Disclosure, not lineage" (#725); embedded fields are scaffold the pipeline reads, its composition role unknown (#1409).3↘
    The archive places this layer of the standard: "IPTC AI metadata" is "Layer 1 metadata", "Disclosure, not lineage", where artifact provenance "operates at the moment of artifact creation" and the dimensions of provenance are independent, each preserved or destroyed "regardless of the others" (#725), and against the reading of provenance as "a field, a tag, a manifest, a credential, separable from the object it documents," #725 holds that "To strip provenance is to change what the meaning *is*" (#725).§22 The archive uses the standard's vocabulary for its own artifacts: Digital Source Type declared as digital capture of a physical original is "the nonsynthetic claim made machine-readable inside the file," the archive's scaffold, "everything machine-readable around the ink," takes in IPTC/XMP/EXIF, and "C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards" as the archive's substrate checksum (#1409).§23 The archive records the same channel as established for extraction and open for composition: IPTC photo metadata "embedded in the file (travels with the image across pages)," "ESTABLISHED as extracted; composition role unknown," and "scaffold the pipeline provably reads" (#1409).§25
  • Who reads it: Google Images shows creator, credit and copyright; the IPTC's inspector shows the rest (User Guide; FAQ; Chrome Web Store).1↘
    Google reads the embedded fields: it "displays three IPTC photo metadata fields, wherever available," telling the viewer the creator, the copyright holder and the credit line (User Guide), a display "introduced by Google in September 2018" (IPTC Guidelines & Support), "Google extracts this information from photos in search results" (FAQ), and the IPTC's browser extension sends a web image to its GetPMD tool, "which will display all metadata embedded in the image file" (Chrome Web Store).§24

🗂️ The record

  • Lifecycle: historical, dated tables, "NOT a current platform audit"; succeeded in method by Metawatch (census record).1↘
    The census record holds the series historical, "the 2019 table is not a 2026 platform measurement," succeeded in method by the IPTC's Metawatch (2026), which it records as a part, with C2PA conformance its neighbour; it tags the series "NOT a current platform audit," leaves the 2016 and 2013 tables, the 2014 software study and the interoperability procedures unchecked, and kinds it a test series (provenance census record).§26
  • Wikipedia: no article on the tests.1↘
    Wikipedia has no article on the tests, and none at the title IPTC Photo Metadata (Wikipedia, as fetched 2026-10-29).§28

🔎 At this address

  • The Overview: composes the standard from the IPTC's pages, leaving out the tests and their losses; no card cites the record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).2↘
    At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry gives the innocent reading first, the standard explained "from the IPTC's own pages," and finds the standard held: "Core and Extension, IIM and XMP, the 2025.1 release and its AI properties are the IPTC's own," with the IPTC named, "no person; no identifier" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§29 It records that the record at the name is the tests and their 2019 losses, that "None of this is in the composition," which "composes the carrier and leaves out the measurement of its erasure," gives the search engines' reading of the data and "omits the loss," heads the 2025.1 properties "AI & Content Provenance" where the IPTC gives them as properties of AI-generated content, and cites no card of the record that landed the same day; it reads the capture as "the baseline for the name" and "the measurement of stripping" as "a second address" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§30

[QUERENT] IPTC photo metadata

[SYSTEM] You can explore the official [IPTC Photo Metadata Standard](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYgHrOzAVgRF_fxxfUoaWdjEmJnXOZUi2mo9AXD-jVEu2IjmL-Wvj_9DMkof04xcPAjsAtWDsUbxAgfu9s_ueEl-GBbSNqzO20Sw3PHeK1jaO3Xww-EWyREarSRCOFKNO33s5) to manage, describe, and protect digital images. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYgHrOzAVgRF_fxxfUoaWdjEmJnXOZUi2mo9AXD-jVEu2IjmL-Wvj_9DMkof04xcPAjsAtWDsUbxAgfu9s_ueEl-GBbSNqzO20Sw3PHeK1jaO3Xww-EWyREarSRCOFKNO33s5), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESfgHrOzAV7usxs9KziO3nXUUjKjLTBtkkXLxpaQ5q-LQ-iC9DAREpVxSUSE4jssaCo7hyXqvHln3UxuGypW2zw5nIH1UbihD4oVeYACNc4Ay7PTwWp73ek4aDjMfKgtiztN4EC4G4R7lxzRv2bPxFqNxPoqFma3g1qGzukw4XmA)]
What is IPTC Photo Metadata?

* Definition: A universally accepted industry standard for embedding administrative, descriptive, and copyright data directly into image files. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdwHrOzAVa6YL90vCdRk54bfdCqyuYvh4CEovCdFgLnEYnW3vbq09ZsykzLkAgXLUGErTkcuY4uCsxb8pXorV__XOQ0JcYHG2Kgd9ZbyoOqFJqcBn9xqzDUyjQakZoE014-xIBDq1rPZXnhrwS1gzyAN-Qx02xwej), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYgHrOzAVgRF_fxxfUoaWdjEmJnXOZUi2mo9AXD-jVEu2IjmL-Wvj_9DMkof04xcPAjsAtWDsUbxAgfu9s_ueEl-GBbSNqzO20Sw3PHeK1jaO3Xww-EWyREarSRCOFKNO33s5)]
* File Formats: Supported across formats like JPEG, TIFF, and PNG, using the [IPTC Core and Extension Schemas](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScAHrOzAVamozPSLuGtmUTmGz7WwmcSatTV8gSXhP-9rIadeE0o5ppLComWGrJdrdV7r9w8ZPg5AcHt7iiTBh6iqnkKCyxuIZn7Zu32WsAykDeM_t3-KZ1Bf5tz_TdNJ6qLmpFvAlGMzKRlW10KxlAkU) as well as Adobe's XMP framework. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScAHrOzAVamozPSLuGtmUTmGz7WwmcSatTV8gSXhP-9rIadeE0o5ppLComWGrJdrdV7r9w8ZPg5AcHt7iiTBh6iqnkKCyxuIZn7Zu32WsAykDeM_t3-KZ1Bf5tz_TdNJ6qLmpFvAlGMzKRlW10KxlAkU), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESeAHrOzAVmh2LShS5MWI7zNanQK48Fy09v-FUYv2fnKOl9Q60zl7NWCKFzXzvAmw_B7hv4YRIkFhcV9ZArqAfLAqhCWvoKppUBtuwrHTa-1FfSdQFDP1Sw-D_tVVoLSju-14i-JNEDTa0OM5CTjm3leteOr04ZieTEQ)]
* Difference from EXIF: While EXIF focuses on technical camera data (shutter speed, ISO, lens settings), IPTC focuses on human-readable details like captions, keywords, and creator credits. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESfwHrOzAV4OaxjMInbnBsTfDNBVPuyfZx3qG_QPAwuA6FUkdWDuhM_hqnEFFXY5HEDP898osmd5eS4Ij5o2s2AvZGP6VBhWtbdEhffhRZTSpOgTS09pI8vTSo1CkN7JlsP-t5GgAO74Oqz2ULN4-gv533xk5Hge5IQL3z66HzPaE)]

Main Metadata Categories

* Descriptive: Includes Alt Text, Headline, Description/Caption, Keywords, and Subject Codes.
* Administrative: Tracks Creation Date, Digital Source Type, Image GUIDs, and registry IDs.
* Rights & Ownership: Stores Creator (Photographer), Copyright Notice, Licensor, and usage terms.
* AI & Content Provenance: Recent standards (such as version 2025.1) include fields for AI System Used, AI System Version, AI Prompt Information, and AI Prompt Writer Name. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFQqPeUMQGV4DdPP7rGUYInuL_LeQuNpiALiUM1bR4IKTJ1rbBFQbcJ_NOqs-g47BgnGnqgaqK5AbUrKuBPZT07T1JmrYBIW5jnrXCwCsozsVyqe1TIiug-6v0v--DpDZvQxWT72pKnr0M-AW97JJJU3qz_0-7ndVehk6RgCvfLSs), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESfgHrOzAV7usxs9KziO3nXUUjKjLTBtkkXLxpaQ5q-LQ-iC9DAREpVxSUSE4jssaCo7hyXqvHln3UxuGypW2zw5nIH1UbihD4oVeYACNc4Ay7PTwWp73ek4aDjMfKgtiztN4EC4G4R7lxzRv2bPxFqNxPoqFma3g1qGzukw4XmA), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdwHrOzAVa6YL90vCdRk54bfdCqyuYvh4CEovCdFgLnEYnW3vbq09ZsykzLkAgXLUGErTkcuY4uCsxb8pXorV__XOQ0JcYHG2Kgd9ZbyoOqFJqcBn9xqzDUyjQakZoE014-xIBDq1rPZXnhrwS1gzyAN-Qx02xwej)]

Key Use Cases

* Digital Asset Management (DAM): Helps archives, news agencies, and stock libraries search and sort massive libraries.
* Search & Google Images: Search engines read embedded IPTC data to display creator information and licensing attributes directly in search results.

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)30 sentences · every one sourced below

The IPTC photo metadata tests

The IPTC photo metadata tests are the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's checks of what image-sharing sites and systems for sharing files and messages do to the metadata embedded in an uploaded photograph: the IPTC "checks about a dozen sites regularly: in 2013, in 2016 and now again in Spring 2019," each time against its own claim that "embedded metadata should not be removed" from shared images (IPTC, Social Media Sites Photo Metadata Test Results 2019), and the provenance census record names the series, gives its operator as the IPTC's Photo Metadata Working Group, and records that it both expresses and tests provenance (provenance census record). Each test uploads an image whose embedded values are all known, "e.g. the latest Reference Image File," checks what the site displays, saves the image with the browser's Save As and downloads it through the system, and asks of each file whether "the embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (in the formats IIM and XMP) of the uploaded image" are "still embedded" (2019 page); the census record keeps the same operations as the transformations tested, embedded metadata inside the file as the carrier, and the site or system as the unit (provenance census record). Four fields are checked on display, "Caption/description, Creator, Copyright Notice, Credit Line (= the 4Cs )" (2019 page), which the census record carries as the relations tested: creation, credit, rights and description (provenance census record).

The IPTC gives the series its origin: users "discovered that when they shared photos via social media sites or systems, their embedded metadata disappeared," and the Working Group "tested 15 social media sites in 2016 and 2013 to understand how image sharing, through upload and download, affects the integrity of embedded metadata" (IPTC, Photo Metadata Research). The research is the IPTC's second activity beside the standard, "IPTC not only defines the standard for photo metadata, but also conducts research about how photo metadata is used and implemented" (Research page), and the IPTC's Photo Metadata page, the composition's first card, says so in the same terms and adds: "The removal of rights information as images are transferred is of particular concern" (IPTC, Photo Metadata). The census record dates the series to 2013, 2016 and Spring 2019, with a software test published in August 2014, counts 15 sites in 2016 and 2013 and about a dozen in 2019, and was read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record).

In the Spring 2019 tables Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash strip the metadata from saved and downloaded files, and on Flickr the "Embedded Creator" is "replaced by account owner" while saved files lose their XMP (2019 page). Among the systems for sharing files and messages, Facebook keeps "A few rights related fields" in IIM and Exif and writes two IIM fields of its own, Twitter strips saved files, and Dropbox and OneDrive pass the original through while their previews save "with stripped off metadata"; Behance's saved files "keep the embedded metadata" (2019 page). The census record keeps the same year and the same losses as its retention results: of eleven image-sharing sites, Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripping, Flickr replacing the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripping on Save As, Facebook keeping a few rights fields (provenance census record). The research page reads the series as showing that some sites "remove embedded information like copyright notes, the name of the creator, the description and more, while others protect photographers’ data better," and that "it is not impossible to preserve metadata in a workflow"; its software study of August 2014 found rights fields in half of the programs tested, retrieval of embedded rights data in two out of three, and two programs that "didn’t support rights metadata at all" (Research page).

The norm the tests measure is the IPTC's own: its User Guide endorses the Embedded Metadata Manifesto, under which "Copyright management information metadata must never be removed from the files," removal being "forbidden by law in many countries," and its minimum set of fields "is not a permission to strip off metadata" (IPTC Photo Metadata User Guide, November 2025). The same guide and the IPTC's Google Images FAQ place the loss also in the sites that host images: a site's "digital asset management system, content management system, image management system or content delivery network may be stripping out embedded metadata fields" (User Guide), the metadata "might be stripped from your images by some software on your site," a DAM, a CMS such as WordPress or Drupal, or a CDN such as Cloudflare (FAQ), and NeededApps' explainer holds that metadata is no "infallible form of copyright protection because it can be removed or modified" (NeededApps). The archive reads the same loss at other carriers and stages: in-pixel metadata "survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss," so the archive's handwritten artifacts carry their metadata three times, "in the pixels + embedded (IPTC/XMP/C2PA) + external" (#1409), and the publication layer's provenance signals, C2PA manifests and structured metadata among them, "are stripped or rendered invisible long before they reach the training corpus. The body text is what survives" (#127).

The object the tests test is a distinct entity, the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard, which "sets the industry standard for administrative, descriptive, and copyright information about images" (IPTC, Photo Metadata): its properties are grouped "into Administrative, Descriptive and Rights-related properties" (Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1) in two schemas, IPTC Core and IPTC Extension, "built on the legacy of the original IPTC-IIM" (IPTC Photo Metadata Standard page), and the census record gives the object they bear on as "the photograph as a file: embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (IIM and XMP)" (provenance census record). Its current release is 2025.1, "including … IPTC Core Metadata Schema 1.5 … IPTC Extension Metadata Schema 1.9" (specification, About the Standard), while the same specification heads its Extension section "IPTC Extension schema 1.8 specifications" (specification, contents and body). Its genealogy runs from the IIM, "developed in the early 1990s by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) to expedite the international exchange of news" (Wikipedia, IPTC Information Interchange Model), whose image properties were embedded as the "IPTC header" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council; Wikipedia, IIM), to XMP, which "has largely superseded IIM's file structure" (Wikipedia, IIM), the IPTC having worked "alongside Adobe" on an implementation that "employs Adobe’s XMP technology" (Standard page); Core fields embedded in both formats must have their values synchronised by the image software (User Guide). The standard leaves the file and the camera to others: how its formats are stored inside image files is "defined by non-IPTC file format standards, such as JPEG/JFIF, TIFF, PNG and more" (Standard page), and the specification "does not include any technical metadata" (specification), the capture data NeededApps assigns to Exif while IPTC metadata "is commonly used to describe, organize and manage images" (NeededApps). The IPTC calls it "the most widely used standard to describe photos, because of its universal acceptance among news agencies, photographers, photo agencies, libraries, museums, and other related industries" (Standard page), Wikipedia "by far IPTC's most widely used standard" for its "nearly universal acceptance among photographers" (Wikipedia, IIM), and its stated uses are "protecting images' copyright and licensing information online" and "managing digital assets" (IPTC, Photo Metadata). Its operator, the International Press Telecommunications Council, is "a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors" that "acts as the global standards body of the news media" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council), and its own conference video marks "20 years of IPTC Photo Metadata" (IPTC, YouTube, title only).

The 2025.1 release, announced by the Working Group on 27 November 2025, adds four properties "for AI-generated content", AI Prompt Information, AI Prompt Writer Name, AI System Used and AI System Version Used, the third defined as "The AI engine and/or the model name used to generate this image" (IPTC news; Standard page), beside the Data Mining property, a "Data mining prohibition or permission, optionally with constraints" (specification). The User Guide gives their purpose, to tell AI-generated images from "regular" ones "to avoid re-training AI models on content that was already generated by a model," and recommends leaving Image Creator empty and setting Digital Source Type to trainedAlgorithmicMedia or compositeSynthetic (User Guide); the announcement records that writing the new properties into its example image "has rendered the C2PA metadata invalid" (IPTC news), and the census record marks the tests "NOT a test of C2PA credentials" (provenance census record). The archive places this layer of the standard: "IPTC AI metadata" is "Layer 1 metadata", "Disclosure, not lineage", where artifact provenance "operates at the moment of artifact creation" and the dimensions of provenance are independent, each preserved or destroyed "regardless of the others" (#725), and against the reading of provenance as "a field, a tag, a manifest, a credential, separable from the object it documents," #725 holds that "To strip provenance is to change what the meaning *is*" (#725). The archive uses the standard's vocabulary for its own artifacts: Digital Source Type declared as digital capture of a physical original is "the nonsynthetic claim made machine-readable inside the file," the archive's scaffold, "everything machine-readable around the ink," takes in IPTC/XMP/EXIF, and "C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards" as the archive's substrate checksum (#1409).

Google reads the embedded fields: it "displays three IPTC photo metadata fields, wherever available," telling the viewer the creator, the copyright holder and the credit line (User Guide), a display "introduced by Google in September 2018" (IPTC Guidelines & Support), "Google extracts this information from photos in search results" (FAQ), and the IPTC's browser extension sends a web image to its GetPMD tool, "which will display all metadata embedded in the image file" (Chrome Web Store). The archive records the same channel as established for extraction and open for composition: IPTC photo metadata "embedded in the file (travels with the image across pages)," "ESTABLISHED as extracted; composition role unknown," and "scaffold the pipeline provably reads" (#1409).

The census record holds the series historical, "the 2019 table is not a 2026 platform measurement," succeeded in method by the IPTC's Metawatch (2026), which it records as a part, with C2PA conformance its neighbour; it tags the series "NOT a current platform audit," leaves the 2016 and 2013 tables, the 2014 software study and the interoperability procedures unchecked, and kinds it a test series (provenance census record). Its organizing question is asked of every entity alike: "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" (provenance census record). Wikipedia has no article on the tests, and none at the title IPTC Photo Metadata (Wikipedia, as fetched 2026-10-29).

At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry gives the innocent reading first, the standard explained "from the IPTC's own pages," and finds the standard held: "Core and Extension, IIM and XMP, the 2025.1 release and its AI properties are the IPTC's own," with the IPTC named, "no person; no identifier" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It records that the record at the name is the tests and their 2019 losses, that "None of this is in the composition," which "composes the carrier and leaves out the measurement of its erasure," gives the search engines' reading of the data and "omits the loss," heads the 2025.1 properties "AI & Content Provenance" where the IPTC gives them as properties of AI-generated content, and cites no card of the record that landed the same day; it reads the capture as "the baseline for the name" and "the measurement of stripping" as "a second address" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)IPTC photo metadata

IPTC Photo Metadata is the IPTC's industry standard for administrative, descriptive and copyright information embedded in image files, in IPTC Core and Extension; the IPTC also tests what sharing sites do to it (IPTC pages; specification).

📐 The standard

  • Release: 2025.1, Core 1.5 and Extension 1.9 (contents say 1.8) (specification).1↘
    The current release, 2025.1, includes Core 1.5 and Extension 1.9, though the specification's contents head the Extension section 1.8 (specification).§2
  • History: IIM in the 1990s, 'IPTC headers', then XMP with Adobe (Wikipedia; Standard page).1↘
    The IPTC developed the IIM in the early 1990s for news exchange; its image fields became the 'IPTC headers', and XMP, implemented with Adobe, has largely superseded IIM's structure, the two kept in sync by software (Wikipedia; Standard page; User Guide).§3
  • Scope: no file-format or technical camera data, unlike Exif (Standard page; NeededApps).1↘
    File formats are defined by non-IPTC standards and technical camera data is excluded, which is where Exif differs (Standard page; specification; NeededApps).§4
  • Use: copyright, licensing, asset management; widely accepted (IPTC; Wikipedia).1↘
    It is called the most widely used photo standard, by near-universal acceptance, and serves copyright, licensing and asset management; its operator is the London consortium of news agencies, whose video marks twenty years of the standard (IPTC; Wikipedia; YouTube).§5
  • AI fields: four 2025.1 properties; C2PA metadata invalidated in the example (IPTC news; User Guide).2↘
    Version 2025.1, released 27 November 2025, adds four properties for AI-generated content, such as AI System Used, beside the Data Mining property (IPTC news; Standard page; specification).§6 For AI-generated images the guide recommends an empty Image Creator and a synthetic Digital Source Type, to avoid re-training on generated content; adding the fields invalidated the example image's C2PA metadata (User Guide; IPTC news).§7
  • Readers: Google Images since 2018; the IPTC inspector and GetPMD (User Guide; FAQ).1↘
    Google Images has displayed creator, credit and copyright from embedded fields since 2018, and the IPTC's inspector and GetPMD show the rest (User Guide; Guidelines; FAQ; Chrome Web Store).§8

🧪 The tests

  • Method: upload, view, Save As, download; the 4Cs (2019 page; Research page).2↘
    The IPTC also researches how photo metadata is used, prompted by users whose embedded metadata disappeared on social media; it tested 15 sites in 2013 and 2016 and about a dozen in 2019 against its claim that embedded metadata should not be removed (Photo Metadata page; Research page; 2019 page).§9 Each test uploads a fully described image, checks the display of caption, creator, copyright notice and credit line, and checks Save As and downloaded files for the embedded Exif and IPTC (2019 page).§10
  • 2019: Pexels, pixabay, Unsplash strip; Flickr replaces the creator; Behance keeps (2019 page).2↘
    In 2019 Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripped saved and downloaded files, Flickr replaced the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripped, Facebook kept a few rights fields, Dropbox and OneDrive previews were stripped, and Behance kept the metadata (2019 page).§11 The research concludes that preserving metadata in a workflow is not impossible; a 2014 software study found rights fields in half the programs (Research page).§12
  • Stripping: DAMs, CMSs and CDNs too; rights metadata must not be removed (User Guide; FAQ; NeededApps).1↘
    The IPTC holds that rights metadata must never be removed and warns that DAMs, CMSs and CDNs may strip it; a third-party explainer adds that metadata can be removed or modified (User Guide; FAQ; NeededApps).§13
  • Wikipedia: no article on the tests.1↘
    Wikipedia has no article on the tests (Wikipedia).§14

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)14 sentences · every one sourced below

IPTC Photo Metadata

IPTC Photo Metadata is the industry standard for administrative, descriptive and copyright information about images, its properties grouped as administrative, descriptive and rights-related in two schemas, Core and Extension, built on the legacy IIM (IPTC pages; specification). The current release, 2025.1, includes Core 1.5 and Extension 1.9, though the specification's contents head the Extension section 1.8 (specification). The IPTC developed the IIM in the early 1990s for news exchange; its image fields became the 'IPTC headers', and XMP, implemented with Adobe, has largely superseded IIM's structure, the two kept in sync by software (Wikipedia; Standard page; User Guide). File formats are defined by non-IPTC standards and technical camera data is excluded, which is where Exif differs (Standard page; specification; NeededApps).

It is called the most widely used photo standard, by near-universal acceptance, and serves copyright, licensing and asset management; its operator is the London consortium of news agencies, whose video marks twenty years of the standard (IPTC; Wikipedia; YouTube). Version 2025.1, released 27 November 2025, adds four properties for AI-generated content, such as AI System Used, beside the Data Mining property (IPTC news; Standard page; specification). For AI-generated images the guide recommends an empty Image Creator and a synthetic Digital Source Type, to avoid re-training on generated content; adding the fields invalidated the example image's C2PA metadata (User Guide; IPTC news).

Google Images has displayed creator, credit and copyright from embedded fields since 2018, and the IPTC's inspector and GetPMD show the rest (User Guide; Guidelines; FAQ; Chrome Web Store).

The IPTC also researches how photo metadata is used, prompted by users whose embedded metadata disappeared on social media; it tested 15 sites in 2013 and 2016 and about a dozen in 2019 against its claim that embedded metadata should not be removed (Photo Metadata page; Research page; 2019 page). Each test uploads a fully described image, checks the display of caption, creator, copyright notice and credit line, and checks Save As and downloaded files for the embedded Exif and IPTC (2019 page). In 2019 Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripped saved and downloaded files, Flickr replaced the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripped, Facebook kept a few rights fields, Dropbox and OneDrive previews were stripped, and Behance kept the metadata (2019 page). The research concludes that preserving metadata in a workflow is not impossible; a 2014 software study found rights fields in half the programs (Research page).

The IPTC holds that rights metadata must never be removed and warns that DAMs, CMSs and CDNs may strip it; a third-party explainer adds that metadata can be removed or modified (User Guide; FAQ; NeededApps). Wikipedia has no article on the tests (Wikipedia).

IPTC Photo Metadata is the industry standard for administrative, descriptive and copyright information about images, its properties grouped as administrative, descriptive and rights-related in two schemas, Core and Extension, built on the legacy IIM (IPTC pages; specification). The current release, 2025.1, includes Core 1.5 and Extension 1.9, though the specification's contents head the Extension section 1.8 (specification). The IPTC developed the IIM in the early 1990s for news exchange; its image fields became the 'IPTC headers', and XMP, implemented with Adobe, has largely superseded IIM's structure, the two kept in sync by software (Wikipedia; Standard page; User Guide). File formats are defined by non-IPTC standards and technical camera data is excluded, which is where Exif differs (Standard page; specification; NeededApps). It is called the most widely used photo standard, by near-universal acceptance, and serves copyright, licensing and asset management; its operator is the London consortium of news agencies, whose video marks twenty years of the standard (IPTC; Wikipedia; YouTube). Version 2025.1, released 27 November 2025, adds four properties for AI-generated content, such as AI System Used, beside the Data Mining property (IPTC news; Standard page; specification). For AI-generated images the guide recommends an empty Image Creator and a synthetic Digital Source Type, to avoid re-training on generated content; adding the fields invalidated the example image's C2PA metadata (User Guide; IPTC news). Google Images has displayed creator, credit and copyright from embedded fields since 2018, and the IPTC's inspector and GetPMD show the rest (User Guide; Guidelines; FAQ; Chrome Web Store). The IPTC also researches how photo metadata is used, prompted by users whose embedded metadata disappeared on social media; it tested 15 sites in 2013 and 2016 and about a dozen in 2019 against its claim that embedded metadata should not be removed (Photo Metadata page; Research page; 2019 page). Each test uploads a fully described image, checks the display of caption, creator, copyright notice and credit line, and checks Save As and downloaded files for the embedded Exif and IPTC (2019 page). In 2019 Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripped saved and downloaded files, Flickr replaced the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripped, Facebook kept a few rights fields, Dropbox and OneDrive previews were stripped, and Behance kept the metadata (2019 page). The research concludes that preserving metadata in a workflow is not impossible; a 2014 software study found rights fields in half the programs (Research page). The IPTC holds that rights metadata must never be removed and warns that DAMs, CMSs and CDNs may strip it; a third-party explainer adds that metadata can be removed or modified (User Guide; FAQ; NeededApps). Wikipedia has no article on the tests (Wikipedia).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1938 words

The IPTC photo metadata tests are the IPTC Photo Metadata Working Group's checks of what image-sharing sites and systems for sharing files and messages do to the metadata embedded in an uploaded photograph: the IPTC "checks about a dozen sites regularly: in 2013, in 2016 and now again in Spring 2019," each time against its own claim that "embedded metadata should not be removed" from shared images (IPTC, Social Media Sites Photo Metadata Test Results 2019), and the provenance census record names the series, gives its operator as the IPTC's Photo Metadata Working Group, and records that it both expresses and tests provenance (provenance census record). Each test uploads an image whose embedded values are all known, "e.g. the latest Reference Image File," checks what the site displays, saves the image with the browser's Save As and downloads it through the system, and asks of each file whether "the embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (in the formats IIM and XMP) of the uploaded image" are "still embedded" (2019 page); the census record keeps the same operations as the transformations tested, embedded metadata inside the file as the carrier, and the site or system as the unit (provenance census record). Four fields are checked on display, "Caption/description, Creator, Copyright Notice, Credit Line (= the 4Cs )" (2019 page), which the census record carries as the relations tested: creation, credit, rights and description (provenance census record). The IPTC gives the series its origin: users "discovered that when they shared photos via social media sites or systems, their embedded metadata disappeared," and the Working Group "tested 15 social media sites in 2016 and 2013 to understand how image sharing, through upload and download, affects the integrity of embedded metadata" (IPTC, Photo Metadata Research). The research is the IPTC's second activity beside the standard, "IPTC not only defines the standard for photo metadata, but also conducts research about how photo metadata is used and implemented" (Research page), and the IPTC's Photo Metadata page, the composition's first card, says so in the same terms and adds: "The removal of rights information as images are transferred is of particular concern" (IPTC, Photo Metadata). The census record dates the series to 2013, 2016 and Spring 2019, with a software test published in August 2014, counts 15 sites in 2016 and 2013 and about a dozen in 2019, and was read on 2026-10-29 (provenance census record). In the Spring 2019 tables Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash strip the metadata from saved and downloaded files, and on Flickr the "Embedded Creator" is "replaced by account owner" while saved files lose their XMP (2019 page). Among the systems for sharing files and messages, Facebook keeps "A few rights related fields" in IIM and Exif and writes two IIM fields of its own, Twitter strips saved files, and Dropbox and OneDrive pass the original through while their previews save "with stripped off metadata"; Behance's saved files "keep the embedded metadata" (2019 page). The census record keeps the same year and the same losses as its retention results: of eleven image-sharing sites, Pexels, pixabay and Unsplash stripping, Flickr replacing the creator with the account owner, Twitter stripping on Save As, Facebook keeping a few rights fields (provenance census record). The research page reads the series as showing that some sites "remove embedded information like copyright notes, the name of the creator, the description and more, while others protect photographers’ data better," and that "it is not impossible to preserve metadata in a workflow"; its software study of August 2014 found rights fields in half of the programs tested, retrieval of embedded rights data in two out of three, and two programs that "didn’t support rights metadata at all" (Research page). The norm the tests measure is the IPTC's own: its User Guide endorses the Embedded Metadata Manifesto, under which "Copyright management information metadata must never be removed from the files," removal being "forbidden by law in many countries," and its minimum set of fields "is not a permission to strip off metadata" (IPTC Photo Metadata User Guide, November 2025). The same guide and the IPTC's Google Images FAQ place the loss also in the sites that host images: a site's "digital asset management system, content management system, image management system or content delivery network may be stripping out embedded metadata fields" (User Guide), the metadata "might be stripped from your images by some software on your site," a DAM, a CMS such as WordPress or Drupal, or a CDN such as Cloudflare (FAQ), and NeededApps' explainer holds that metadata is no "infallible form of copyright protection because it can be removed or modified" (NeededApps). The archive reads the same loss at other carriers and stages: in-pixel metadata "survives screenshot, rehosting, filename change, metadata stripping, PDF embedding, and sidecar loss," so the archive's handwritten artifacts carry their metadata three times, "in the pixels + embedded (IPTC/XMP/C2PA) + external" (#1409), and the publication layer's provenance signals, C2PA manifests and structured metadata among them, "are stripped or rendered invisible long before they reach the training corpus. The body text is what survives" (#127). The object the tests test is a distinct entity, the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard, which "sets the industry standard for administrative, descriptive, and copyright information about images" (IPTC, Photo Metadata): its properties are grouped "into Administrative, Descriptive and Rights-related properties" (Photo Metadata Standard 2025.1) in two schemas, IPTC Core and IPTC Extension, "built on the legacy of the original IPTC-IIM" (IPTC Photo Metadata Standard page), and the census record gives the object they bear on as "the photograph as a file: embedded Exif and IPTC metadata (IIM and XMP)" (provenance census record). Its current release is 2025.1, "including … IPTC Core Metadata Schema 1.5 … IPTC Extension Metadata Schema 1.9" (specification, About the Standard), while the same specification heads its Extension section "IPTC Extension schema 1.8 specifications" (specification, contents and body). Its genealogy runs from the IIM, "developed in the early 1990s by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) to expedite the international exchange of news" (Wikipedia, IPTC Information Interchange Model), whose image properties were embedded as the "IPTC header" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council; Wikipedia, IIM), to XMP, which "has largely superseded IIM's file structure" (Wikipedia, IIM), the IPTC having worked "alongside Adobe" on an implementation that "employs Adobe’s XMP technology" (Standard page); Core fields embedded in both formats must have their values synchronised by the image software (User Guide). The standard leaves the file and the camera to others: how its formats are stored inside image files is "defined by non-IPTC file format standards, such as JPEG/JFIF, TIFF, PNG and more" (Standard page), and the specification "does not include any technical metadata" (specification), the capture data NeededApps assigns to Exif while IPTC metadata "is commonly used to describe, organize and manage images" (NeededApps). The IPTC calls it "the most widely used standard to describe photos, because of its universal acceptance among news agencies, photographers, photo agencies, libraries, museums, and other related industries" (Standard page), Wikipedia "by far IPTC's most widely used standard" for its "nearly universal acceptance among photographers" (Wikipedia, IIM), and its stated uses are "protecting images' copyright and licensing information online" and "managing digital assets" (IPTC, Photo Metadata). Its operator, the International Press Telecommunications Council, is "a consortium of the world's major news agencies, other news providers and news industry vendors" that "acts as the global standards body of the news media" (Wikipedia, International Press Telecommunications Council), and its own conference video marks "20 years of IPTC Photo Metadata" (IPTC, YouTube, title only). The 2025.1 release, announced by the Working Group on 27 November 2025, adds four properties "for AI-generated content", AI Prompt Information, AI Prompt Writer Name, AI System Used and AI System Version Used, the third defined as "The AI engine and/or the model name used to generate this image" (IPTC news; Standard page), beside the Data Mining property, a "Data mining prohibition or permission, optionally with constraints" (specification). The User Guide gives their purpose, to tell AI-generated images from "regular" ones "to avoid re-training AI models on content that was already generated by a model," and recommends leaving Image Creator empty and setting Digital Source Type to trainedAlgorithmicMedia or compositeSynthetic (User Guide); the announcement records that writing the new properties into its example image "has rendered the C2PA metadata invalid" (IPTC news), and the census record marks the tests "NOT a test of C2PA credentials" (provenance census record). The archive places this layer of the standard: "IPTC AI metadata" is "Layer 1 metadata", "Disclosure, not lineage", where artifact provenance "operates at the moment of artifact creation" and the dimensions of provenance are independent, each preserved or destroyed "regardless of the others" (#725), and against the reading of provenance as "a field, a tag, a manifest, a credential, separable from the object it documents," #725 holds that "To strip provenance is to change what the meaning is" (#725). The archive uses the standard's vocabulary for its own artifacts: Digital Source Type declared as digital capture of a physical original is "the nonsynthetic claim made machine-readable inside the file," the archive's scaffold, "everything machine-readable around the ink," takes in IPTC/XMP/EXIF, and "C2PA, FADGI, and IPTC provenance vocabularies are the same insight arriving as standards" as the archive's substrate checksum (#1409). Google reads the embedded fields: it "displays three IPTC photo metadata fields, wherever available," telling the viewer the creator, the copyright holder and the credit line (User Guide), a display "introduced by Google in September 2018" (IPTC Guidelines & Support), "Google extracts this information from photos in search results" (FAQ), and the IPTC's browser extension sends a web image to its GetPMD tool, "which will display all metadata embedded in the image file" (Chrome Web Store). The archive records the same channel as established for extraction and open for composition: IPTC photo metadata "embedded in the file (travels with the image across pages)," "ESTABLISHED as extracted; composition role unknown," and "scaffold the pipeline provably reads" (#1409). The census record holds the series historical, "the 2019 table is not a 2026 platform measurement," succeeded in method by the IPTC's Metawatch (2026), which it records as a part, with C2PA conformance its neighbour; it tags the series "NOT a current platform audit," leaves the 2016 and 2013 tables, the 2014 software study and the interoperability procedures unchecked, and kinds it a test series (provenance census record). Its organizing question is asked of every entity alike: "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" (provenance census record). Wikipedia has no article on the tests, and none at the title IPTC Photo Metadata (Wikipedia, as fetched 2026-10-29). At the bare name on Google's AI Overview the Capture Registry gives the innocent reading first, the standard explained "from the IPTC's own pages," and finds the standard held: "Core and Extension, IIM and XMP, the 2025.1 release and its AI properties are the IPTC's own," with the IPTC named, "no person; no identifier" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It records that the record at the name is the tests and their 2019 losses, that "None of this is in the composition," which "composes the carrier and leaves out the measurement of its erasure," gives the search engines' reading of the data and "omits the loss," heads the 2025.1 properties "AI & Content Provenance" where the IPTC gives them as properties of AI-generated content, and cites no card of the record that landed the same day; it reads the capture as "the baseline for the name" and "the measurement of stripping" as "a second address" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).
